sentences.text: The name Dicraeosaurus refers to the distinctive neural spines located on the back of the animal's neck, a feature that set it apart from most other diplodocoids which typically possessed longer necks and smaller heads.

Unlike its relatives, this dinosaur had a relatively short, wide neck containing 12 unusually short vertebrae, measuring about 2.4 meters in length out of a total body length that could reach up to 20 meters.
The animal stood up to 6 meters tall, and while some estimates place its weight at approximately 15 tons, other studies suggest a range between 10 and 40 tons.
Its neck vertebrae contained numerous air spaces, especially developed at the back of the neck, contributing to the structure's unique anatomy.
Numerous attempts to estimate its mass yielded varied results, placing the weight of D. hansemanni between 10 and 40 tons.
The tail of Dicraeosaurus, which acted like a whip, could be used for defense or to make loud sounds.
The two species of Dicraeosaurus did not live together, as they were found in different geological layers spanning from the Oxfordian to the Tithonian.
The first fossils of Dicraeosaurus were described by paleontologist Werner Janensch in 1914.
Fossils of Dicraeosaurus were found in the Tendaguru Formation in Tanzania and possibly in Kazdi, Zimbabwe.
Researchers suggest the tall neural spines likely provided attachment points for muscles, serving as insertion points for powerful neck muscles.

Researchers Martin and colleagues suggest that a cervical ligament played a decisive role in maintaining the neck position, allowing the animal to maintain an upright neck and bent head while walking on extended legs.
Some experts believe the neck of Dicraeosaurus could have been inclined, though a horizontal position is not excluded.
The peg-shaped teeth of Dicraeosaurus were ideal for feeding on plants, enabling it to eat hard foods like cycads thanks to its wide teeth.

While some authors suggest the skull structure indicates biting movements adapted for cutting food, others interpret it as front-to-back movements typical of earlier sauropods adapted for pulling food.

In 2008, Lehman and Woodward estimated that a mature adult Dicraeosaurus lived for 11 to 22 years and grew at an average rate of 227 to 455 kg per year, growing rapidly and without interruption to its maximum size, reaching sexual maturity at 80% of that maximum size.
Calculations indicate that Dicraeosaurus contained 974 liters of air, with a 48-kilogram heart pumping 641 liters of blood at a rate of 23 beats per minute.
The genus Dicraeosaurus has been synonymized with Issasaurus, Mtotosaurus, Nyororosaurus, and Selimanosaurus.
Since 1991, Dicraeosaurus has been classified in the family Dicraeosauridae, part of the superfamily Diplodocoidea, a family believed to be more evolutionarily advanced than the family Diplodocidae.
A 2005 study by Rauhut confirmed that Dicraeosaurus is monophyletic and more closely related to Brachytrachelopan than to Amargasaurus.

Dicraeosaurus hansemanni lived between the Oxfordian and Kimeridgian stages, while D. sattleri lived during the Tithonian stage, with the genus living from the Oxfordian to the Tithonian stages, approximately 161.5 to 143.1 million years ago.
Dicraeosaurus was a herbivore that did not compete with other dinosaurs for food.
The hypothesis that Dicraeosaurus stopped growing earlier than its relatives is supported by the poor pneumatization of its bones.
The long neck of sauropods like Dicraeosaurus may have evolved as a result of sexual selection.
A 2026 study by Beeston et al. included Dicraeosaurus sattleri in an analysis of caudal vertebrae that found at least five independent origins or reversals of pneumaticity in Neosauropoda.
